newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican rebels vow to fight on despite elections.
newsitem.headline: Mexican rebels vow to fight on despite elections.

text.p: Mexico's Marxist rebels have vowed to press their fight against the government despite recent elections viewed as the cleanest in the country's history.

In a statement obtained by Reuters on Friday, the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) praised Mexico's July 6 midterm elections as a step toward democracy but added that more needed to be done before the guerrillas laid down their arms.

"During the recent electoral process, although it was not totally clean on a national or state level, there was an advance on the part of democratic forces," EPR Commander Hermenegildo said in the statement, dated July 17 and signed from the southwestern Mexican state of Guerrero.

"(But) an electoral struggle and a people ready to defend themselves with guns are by no means exclusive -- they complement one another because they both aim at the same goal of transforming the country," Hermenegildo added.

Voters effectively ended Mexico's one-party system on July 6 by stripping the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) of control of the lower house of Congress and the capital city. The PRI has ruled Mexico since 1929.
Political observers agreed the vote was free from the PRI's historic tactics of foul play, although opposition parties protested against alleged fraud in several state races.

Rebels declared a ceasefire before the vote but earlier this week said they would resume revolutionary activity. Some 35 people have died since the EPR launched attacks on army and police in June 1996.
The guerrillas, who operate in several Mexican states, said repressive acts by the Mexican government had belied its new democratic face and shown the need for continued rebellion.

They accused the government of torturing and "disappearing" one of its fighters and three social activists in Guerrero and of failing to bring former state officials to justice for a 1995 peasant massacre.
"Much remains to be done because real democracy exists in the way those who govern exercise their power, the way society participates in decisions, the way wealth is distributed," the statement said.
"In a real democracy, the government uses arguments, plebiscites and a vote; there is no space for coercion, repression, intimidation, impunity and corruption," it added.
Rebels said political parties in Mexico still competed in uneven conditions in terms of financing, access to the media and state support.
